newsitem.title: UK: British party wants decimal time, ban on winter.
newsitem.headline: British party wants decimal time, ban on winter.

text.p: Britain's longest-serving party leader, Screaming Lord Sutch, launched an election manifesto for his Monster Raving Loony Party on Wednesday that included plans to abolish January and February to make winter shorter.

Wearing his trademark tiger-striped lurex suit and leopard skin top hat, Sutch and other members of the Loony Party held a news conference on Westminster Bridge beside the Houses of Parliament to announce his policies for the next election.
Bellowing above the noise of traffic and flanked by a yellow-clad Banana Man and John Major look-alike, Sutch, 53, pledged to give a million pounds ($1.5 million) to everyone who voted for him.
This would be made possible by turning Britain into a tax haven and undercutting Switzerland. "We will be knee-deep in money," declared the self-ennobled Sutch.
The slogan "Vote for insanity -- you know it makes sense" gives a taste of the party platform for an election due by May.
Under Sutch, dogs would have to eat flourescent food to avoid the danger of treading in dog mess at night.
Other manifesto proposals included plans to decimalise time to make life simpler "especially when you're hungover, late for work, and trying to figure out a 24-hour timetable."
There would be 10 days to a week, 10 hours to the day, 100 minutes to the hour and 100 seconds to the minute.
Additional perks for boozy Britons would include a new law banning work before lunchtime, "because it's far too difficult."
Nationalistic Scots who want their own parliament, would be lent the London-based one, which would be put on wheels.
The space left by it in Westminster would be filled by a giant amusement park to rival Paris's EuroDisney.

Sutch, who has been on the campaign trail for 33 years, has fought 37 election campaigns, including local polls, but has never won a seat. He was joined by a handful of other Loony Party candidates at the last election.
When he is not on the campaign trail, he makes his living as the leader of a rock and roll band, The Savages, which, like his political career, exists on the fringes of glory.
The Rolling Stones once played as support band to The Savages and the late Keith Moon of The Who was once Sutch's drummer.
Sutch was threatened with bankruptcy last year. To ease his financial troubles, his 500 pound ($782.2) mandatory deposit to stand for parliament is being paid by a bookmaking firm.
Sutch's best election performance was in 1994, when he 1,114 votes in a by-election in Rotherham northwest England.
In the last general election in 1992, he won 726 votes.
